analysis.one_liner: Repeals the petroleum and chemical tax that pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites.
analysis.headline: The bill would end the Superfund cleanup tax starting January 2026, saving oil and chemical companies roughly a billion dollars a year while leaving toxic-site cleanup to general taxpayers; it sits without action in the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill shuts off the excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that feeds the Superfund trust fund — the fund Congress uses to clean up the country's most dangerous toxic waste sites. It would end the tax after December 31, 2025, retroactively, and cut off the Treasury advances that back the fund. Pump prices would fall by only a fraction of a cent per gallon, while the fund loses its dedicated income and cleanup costs fall back on ordinary taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil producers, refiners, and petrochemical companies that pay the per-barrel tax. They keep the money that currently funds toxic-waste cleanup. Motorists would see a tiny pump-price drop — the tax works out to well under a penny per gallon.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on petroleum products after December 31, 2025, retroactive to January 1, 2026 [S2].

Also terminates the Treasury's authority to make advances to the Superfund trust fund, striking the existing December 31, 2032 endpoint and replacing it with quarterly repayment from unobligated fund balances [S2].
The tax is levied per barrel of crude oil and petroleum products, so the retail price effect is a fraction of a cent per gallon.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers, who would have to cover toxic-waste cleanups from general revenue once the fund's dedicated income stops, and communities near Superfund sites, where cleanup could slow or be left unfunded.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

drawbacks.text: The Superfund trust fund loses its dedicated revenue stream, so the federal government's main mechanism for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites is left unfunded, with costs shifted to the general treasury [S2].
The repeal is retroactive to January 1, 2026, so taxes already collected in the current year would be subject to refund, reducing federal revenue further [S2].

The bill amends trust fund law to require quarterly repayments from unobligated fund amounts until repaid in full, narrowing the fund's financial flexibility before it even stops receiving dedicated income [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is a pump price cut of less than a penny per gallon, which is barely noticeable. The cost is the loss of dedicated funding for cleaning up hazardous waste sites — a program that protects neighborhoods, water supplies, and public health. The trade strongly favors the companies that pay the tax over the public it protects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and there has been no markup, no vote, and no floor action since.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Carey introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, joined by five Republican cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on February 12, 2026 [S4].
No further legislative action has been recorded; the bill has not been scheduled for a committee markup or a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet — the bill has not moved, so the excise tax remains in place and the Superfund trust fund keeps receiving its dedicated money.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill has not advanced

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Republicans, all from the House; no Democrat has signed on and the bill sits in committee.

industries.note: The Superfund excise is charged per barrel of crude and petroleum products, so repeal directly saves oil companies money. Their savings come from money that would otherwise fund toxic-waste cleanups, and the public price relief is a fraction of a cent per gallon.
These companies pay the same hazardous substance tax on chemicals; repeal removes it, shifting cleanup costs to general taxpayers.
The bill strips the trust fund of its dedicated revenue and cuts off Treasury advances, leaving cleanups dependent on general appropriations or unfunded entirely.

analysis.trajectory: With a single Ways and Means referral, no markup, and five cosponsors after months in session, the bill is unlikely to reach the House floor this Congress. Most tax bills referred to committee without leadership support die quietly at this stage.
